summary:
Go/No-Go is a free browser game where you run a robotic science mission from start to finish, the way real NASA missions are designed. You choose a destination (Earth orbit, the Moon, Mars, Jupiter or Saturn), then build the spacecraft at four engineering stations: rocket, power, science instruments and communications. Every choice trades mass, power, cost, data and risk. Before launch, each flight controller calls "GO" or "NO-GO" and explains any problem in plain English. You then fly the launch, dodge space debris, and operate the spacecraft from a 3D Mission Control room while problems like solar storms and data overflows strike. At the end you are scored on science, survival and budget, and the game shows which real NASA mission your design most resembles, such as Juno, Cassini or MAVEN.

The game follows the real mission-design process from NASA guides, with real physics kept in proportion: sunlight fading with distance, rockets carrying less to far planets, and weaker signals from deep space. It makes mission design easy to understand for anyone in 15 minutes, with no install.
details:
Pitch video: https://youtu.be/4eM1uKifvnQ

Slides: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1aMjcv0X1dQtnjaeNa6ixtF84jSUAbbalK_J3tpXMhBg

Play in your browser: https://rashedutm.github.io/Go-No-Go/

Source code: https://github.com/rashedutm/Go-No-Go

WHAT IT DOES

Go/No-Go follows the same path a real science mission takes:

1. Mission select: choose a target (Earth orbit, Moon, Mars, Jupiter or Saturn) and a difficulty (Cadet, Flight or Director).

2. Briefing: the science goal, the budget, and conditions at the destination such as sunlight, distance and radiation.

3. Hangar (design): four stations, one for each mission segment.

- Mission Director: rocket and mission length.

- Spacecraft Engineer: frame, power (solar panels or RTG), battery and radiation shielding.

- Science Lead: science instruments.

- Comms & Ops: antenna, memory and ground-station hours.

4. Launch poll: each flight controller checks the design and calls GO or NO-GO, explaining any problem in plain English.

5. Launch: fly the spacecraft to its destination and steer around space debris and asteroids. Every hit costs health.

6. Mission Control: walk around a 3D control room and keep the mission alive at the power, thermal, comms and science consoles while random events happen (solar storms, dust, data overflow, comms blackouts). Time can run from 1x to 4x.

7. Debrief: a score for science, survival and budget, 1 to 3 stars, and the real NASA mission (Landsat 9, PACE, LRO, MRO, MAVEN, Juno, Europa Clipper or Cassini) that your design is most like.

HOW IT WORKS

The game is built around the real process in NASA's SmallSat Institute guide "Design and Develop Science Missions": need, concept, requirements, design, review and operations. The four hangar stations match the four mission segments, and the Go/No-Go poll is a simplified design review. The physics is simplified but kept in real proportion:

- Solar power falls with distance squared, so panels that work at Earth fail at Saturn, where you need an RTG, like Cassini.

- Rockets carry much less mass to far planets, so a heavy spacecraft needs a bigger rocket and more budget.

- The data rate falls with distance, so a far mission needs a big antenna, more memory and more ground-station time.

- Jupiter's radiation needs shielding, like Juno's titanium vault.

Players learn these trade-offs by trying, failing and trying again, not by reading.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- No install: it runs in Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Brave and Safari, and shows NASA facts while it loads.

- Every part and every NO-GO call has a plain-English explanation.

- Three difficulty levels, from first-time players to players who want a real challenge.

- Each run ends by linking the player's design to a real NASA mission, encouraging them to look it up.

We hope teachers and students use it as a 15-minute introduction to how space missions are designed, and that it makes real missions feel understandable and exciting.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Instead of reading about mission design, you become the team. You make the trade-offs, face the launch poll, and live with your choices in Mission Control. A NO-GO is not a game over; it is the moment you learn why real engineers made the choices they did.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

- Godot Engine 4.7 (GDScript), exported to WebAssembly / WebGL.

- Hosted on GitHub Pages.

- Mission data (parts, rockets, missions, events and real-mission matches) stored in JSON files.

- Python for build tools, and a custom HTML loading page.

- Claude (Anthropic) was used as an SI assistant for coding, debugging and writing, and SI-assisted code files are marked with a header comment. The background music and alert sounds were generated in code. No NASA logos are used.
